title: A workshop's late repairs

blocks.text: A machine workshop has a pool of mechanics. Each repair needs some mechanics for some days, has a due day, and costs a penalty for every day it finishes after its due day (a customer's machine standing idle). Finishing early earns nothing. Days are numbered from 0, and a job that starts on day `s` and takes `d` days finishes at `s + d`.

Write `least_penalty(jobs, mechanics, horizon)` in `workshop.py`. `jobs` maps a repair to `(days, mechanics_needed, due, penalty_per_day)`. Return `(total, start)`: the smallest total penalty, and each job's start day in a plan that achieves it. All work must end by day `horizon`. Every instance in the tests has a plan.
The model, with $`J`$ the jobs, $`d_j`$, $`m_j`$, $`\delta_j`$ and $`p_j`$ their days, mechanics, due day and daily penalty, $`M`$ the mechanics and $`H`$ the horizon:
The (mechanics) rows are one cumulative constraint; each (late) row is one `add_max_equality`. The tests check the plan you return and the total, so any optimal plan passes. About twenty lines.

from __future__ import annotations

from ortools.sat.python import cp_model


def least_penalty(jobs: dict[str, tuple[int, int, int, int]], mechanics: int,
                  horizon: int) -> tuple[int, dict[str, int]]:
    """(least total penalty, start day of each job) under a pool of mechanics."""
    model = cp_model.CpModel()
    start, late, intervals, demands = {}, {}, [], []
    for name, (days, need, due, _) in jobs.items():
        start[name] = model.new_int_var(0, horizon - days, f"start_{name}")
        intervals.append(model.new_fixed_size_interval_var(start[name], days, f"repair_{name}"))
        demands.append(need)
        late[name] = model.new_int_var(0, horizon, f"late_{name}")
        model.add_max_equality(late[name], [0, start[name] + days - due])
    model.add_cumulative(intervals, demands, mechanics)
    model.minimize(sum(penalty * late[name] for name, (_, _, _, penalty) in jobs.items()))
    solver = cp_model.CpSolver()
    solver.parameters.num_workers = 1
    solver.solve(model)
    return round(solver.objective_value), {name: solver.value(start[name]) for name in jobs}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(least_penalty({"lathe": (3, 1, 3, 5), "press": (2, 2, 4, 9), "pump": (2, 1, 2, 1)}, 2, 20))

cases.says: when every job can finish by its due day, the penalty is 0 and every job ends on time
every job gets a whole-number start day and ends by the horizon
a job that ends before its due day adds nothing, and cannot pay for another job's lateness
when one of two jobs must be late, the one with the smaller daily penalty waits

origin.section: Lateness Is max(0, end − due), and Its Weight Is the Risk Carried

concepts: due weeks that cannot all be met make the model infeasible as rules, so they belong in the objective
lateness is the max of 0 and end minus due, weighted by the risk of each week late
